concepts.title: What Statistics Really Is
concepts.learning_goal: Understand statistics as collecting, organizing, and making sense of data to answer questions instead of guessing.
concepts.key_idea: Statistics turns messy raw facts into clear insight so we can see patterns and make smart decisions.
concepts.suggested_example: A shop owner notes daily sales for a month to see which snack sells fastest instead of guessing.
concepts.check_prompt: In one short sentence, what problem does statistics help us solve?

concepts.title: Descriptive Statistics
concepts.learning_goal: Understand descriptive statistics as summarizing only the exact data you already have.
concepts.key_idea: Descriptive statistics simply organizes and summarizes the exact data in front of you—nothing beyond it.
concepts.suggested_example: Finding the average score or highest score of the 40 students in your own class.
concepts.check_prompt: If a teacher finds the highest and lowest scores in her class of 40 students, is she describing her data or guessing about another school?

concepts.title: Inferential Statistics
concepts.learning_goal: Understand inferential statistics as using a small sample to draw conclusions about a much larger group.
concepts.key_idea: Inferential statistics goes a step further: you study a small group and use it to make an educated conclusion about a bigger group you didn't measure.
concepts.suggested_example: Tasting 5 mangoes from a truckload to judge whether the whole truck is sweet.
concepts.check_prompt: If you ask 20 students at your faculty about their favorite course and conclude most students on campus agree, is that descriptive or inferential?

concepts.title: Population vs. Sample
concepts.learning_goal: Tell the difference between a population (every member of interest) and a sample (the smaller portion actually studied).
concepts.key_idea: A population is the entire group you care about; a sample is the smaller slice you actually inspect.
concepts.suggested_example: All 10,000 students at a university are the population; 200 surveyed students are the sample.
concepts.check_prompt: If you ask 25 classmates how much data they buy weekly to learn about your whole department, which group is the sample?

concepts.title: Qualitative vs. Quantitative Data
concepts.learning_goal: Classify data as qualitative (categories/labels) or quantitative (meaningful numbers).
concepts.key_idea: Qualitative data gives labels or categories, while quantitative data gives numerical counts or measurements.
concepts.suggested_example: Your favorite phone brand is qualitative; your exam score is quantitative.
concepts.check_prompt: Between a student's blood group (O, A, B) and their height in centimeters, which one is quantitative?

concepts.title: Discrete vs. Continuous Data
concepts.learning_goal: Separate countable whole-step data (discrete) from measured data with decimals in between (continuous).
concepts.key_idea: Discrete data comes from counting whole steps (like 1, 2, 3 people); continuous data comes from measuring and can take values in between (like 1.72 meters).
concepts.suggested_example: The number of passengers in a bus is discrete; the exact weight of a bag of rice is continuous.
concepts.check_prompt: Is the number of goals scored in a football match discrete or continuous, and why?

concepts.title: Raw Data & Frequency Tables
concepts.learning_goal: Understand how a frequency table turns an unsorted list of raw data into clear counts.
concepts.key_idea: A frequency table lists each value or category alongside how many times it appears.
concepts.suggested_example: Writing 'A: 4, B: 7, C: 5' instead of staring at 16 scattered quiz grades.
concepts.check_prompt: If 5 students pick their drink as Tea, Coffee, Tea, Water, Tea, what is the frequency of Tea?

concepts.title: Grouped Frequency Distributions
concepts.learning_goal: Understand why we group wide ranges of numerical data into class intervals.
concepts.key_idea: When numbers span a wide range, we group them into neat ranges called class intervals (like 40-49, 50-59) so patterns pop out.
concepts.suggested_example: Grouping 100 exam scores into 10-point bands instead of listing every score from 0 to 100.
concepts.check_prompt: Why is grouping 100 exam scores into bands like 50-59 and 60-69 better than listing every individual number?

concepts.title: Choosing the Right Chart
concepts.learning_goal: Match basic charts (bar chart vs. histogram) to categorical or grouped numerical data.
concepts.key_idea: Bar charts show separate categories with gaps between bars, while histograms show continuous numerical intervals with bars touching.
concepts.suggested_example: A bar chart for favorite drinks; a histogram for student heights grouped into intervals.
concepts.check_prompt: To display how many students walk, bike, or take a bus, should we use a bar chart or a histogram?

concepts.title: The Arithmetic Mean
concepts.learning_goal: Compute the arithmetic mean and see how one extreme value pulls it.
concepts.key_idea: The mean adds all values and divides equally by how many there are—so one giant number can pull the whole average upward.
concepts.check_prompt: What is the mean of 2, 4, and 6—and what happens to it if we change 6 to 60?

concepts.title: The Median
concepts.learning_goal: Find the median by ordering values first and understand why it resists outliers.
concepts.key_idea: The median is the middle value after sorting numbers from smallest to largest, so extreme ends don't disturb it.
concepts.suggested_example: In 2, 5, 9, 10, 100, the middle number is 9 even with 100 at the end.
concepts.check_prompt: What is the median of 12, 3, 7, 15, 5? (Remember to sort them first!)

concepts.title: The Mode
concepts.learning_goal: Identify the mode and see why it works even for non-number data.
concepts.key_idea: The mode is simply the value that appears most often—and it even works for categories like colors or shoe sizes.
concepts.suggested_example: In shoe sizes 39, 41, 41, 42, 41, the mode is 41.
concepts.check_prompt: In [Blue, Red, Blue, Green, Blue], what is the mode, and why can't we find a mean here?

concepts.title: Choosing Mean, Median, or Mode
concepts.learning_goal: Choose between mean, median, and mode depending on outliers or categories.
concepts.key_idea: Use mean for balanced numbers, median when extreme outliers exist, and mode for the most popular category.
concepts.suggested_example: In a street where 9 workers earn normal wages and 1 billionaire lives, the median shows the typical income honestly.
concepts.check_prompt: If 5 friends have pocket money of 10, 12, 11, 13, and 500, should we use the mean or median to show a typical amount?

concepts.title: Why Spread Matters & The Range
concepts.learning_goal: See why averages alone can mislead and compute the range (max - min).
concepts.key_idea: Two classes can share the same average of 60 while one is tightly packed and the other is wildly spread out; the range (largest minus smallest) gives a quick look at spread.
concepts.suggested_example: Scores [58, 60, 62] have range 4, while [20, 60, 100] have range 80, even though both average 60.

concepts.title: Deviations from the Mean
concepts.learning_goal: Understand how far each score sits from the mean and why signed deviations cancel to zero.
concepts.key_idea: A deviation (value minus mean) shows how far above or below average a score sits, and positive and negative deviations always cancel out to zero.
concepts.suggested_example: For [2, 4, 6] with mean 4, the deviations are -2, 0, and +2, which add up to 0.
concepts.check_prompt: For [3, 5, 7] where the mean is 5, what are the three deviations from 5?

concepts.title: Variance Intuition
concepts.learning_goal: Understand why we square deviations before averaging them to get the variance.
concepts.key_idea: Because positive and negative deviations cancel to zero, we square each deviation first (making all positive) and average them—that is the variance.
concepts.suggested_example: For deviations -2, 0, +2, squaring turns them into 4, 0, 4, so they no longer cancel out.
concepts.check_prompt: In plain words, why do we square the deviations when calculating variance?

concepts.title: Standard Deviation
concepts.learning_goal: Understand standard deviation as the square root of variance, bringing spread back to original units.
concepts.key_idea: Squaring deviations leaves us in squared units (like squared scores), so taking the square root brings us back to normal units—giving the typical distance from the mean.
concepts.suggested_example: If heights are in cm, variance is in cm squared, so taking the square root gives standard deviation back in cm.
concepts.check_prompt: Why do we take the square root of the variance to get the standard deviation?

concepts.title: Quartiles & Interquartile Range (IQR)
concepts.learning_goal: Understand IQR (Q3 - Q1) as the spread of the middle 50% of ordered data.
concepts.key_idea: Quartiles split sorted data into four quarters, and IQR (Q3 minus Q1) measures how spread out the middle half is while ignoring wild outliers.
concepts.suggested_example: Looking at the middle 50% of clinic waiting times avoids distortion from one rare 5-hour emergency delay.
concepts.check_prompt: Why is IQR often safer than the full Range when data has one extreme outlier?
